figures.caption: The Shadow Dexterous Hand holding a light bulb in 2007. Each fingertip is a contact whose geometry and friction a simulator must get right; a modified Shadow hand ran the Rubik's cube policy trained with automatic domain randomization.
figures.credit: Photo: Richard Greenhill and Hugo Elias, Shadow Robot Company / Wikimedia Commons. Licence: CC BY-SA 3.0.

figures.alt: Two panels: real robot evaluation, labelled expensive, slow and difficult to reproduce, with photographs of a robot arm at a table; and simulated evaluation, labelled cheap, scalable and fully reproducible, with matching simulated views.
figures.caption: A cheaper evaluator is useful only if it agrees with reality. SIMPLER builds simulated scenes matched to real ones and checks whether simulated policy performance correlates with real performance; a learned simulator should meet the same test.
figures.credit: Paper figure: Xuanlin Li et al. / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: A grid of video frames of a robot arm pushing objects at steps 0, 8, 14, 21 and 29, with rows for ground truth and five rollout methods; red boxes mark misaligned and blurred frames, and the last row is marked aligned.
figures.caption: Autoregressive rollouts can drift in ways one frame hides. On BAIR robot pushing, the RoboWorld authors mark other forcing schemes misaligned or blurred within 29 steps, while their step forcing stays aligned with the ground truth.
figures.credit: Paper figure: Byeongguk Jeon et al. / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: A diagram of RoboArena: a pool of generalist policies feeds a ring of photographed robot workstations, each running pairwise comparisons on its own task, which aggregate into a ranked score table.
figures.caption: RoboArena ranks policies from double-blind pairwise trials that many evaluators run on their own scenes and tasks. More than 600 real-robot episodes on the DROID platform ranked seven generalist policies.
figures.credit: Paper figure: Pranav Atreya et al. / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: A rendered kitchen table crowded with hundreds of 3D objects: fruit, vegetables, meat, bottles, cans, cups, cookware and packaged food.
figures.caption: Generative simulation authors content and leaves dynamics to the physics engine. RoboCasa's library holds 2,509 objects in 153 categories, drawn from Objaverse and the text-to-3D service Luma.ai; a small subset is shown here.
figures.credit: Paper figure: Soroush Nasiriany et al. / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: A grid of rendered simulated kitchens in different layouts and styles, each with a robot standing among cabinets, counters and appliances.
figures.caption: Simulation lets a team test policies across many environments before touching hardware. Rendered RoboCasa kitchens, each holding a simulated robot among varied layouts and styles.
figures.credit: Paper figure: Soroush Nasiriany et al. / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: Three pairs of frame strips for the instructions grasp the blue block and rotate it right, put the broccoli onto the plate, and open the drawer; green-framed ground-truth frames sit above blue-framed predicted frames.
figures.caption: A video world model predicts future frames of a robot task from the current view and a language instruction. GR-1's predicted frames (blue) beneath the ground truth (green) for three instructions.
figures.credit: Paper figure: Hongtao Wu et al. / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: Four groups of tabletop photographs of a robot arm among household objects, labelled Basic Settings, Unseen Backgrounds, Unseen Environments and Unseen Manipulation.
figures.caption: GR-2 pre-trains on web-scale video, then fine-tunes on robot data to generate video and predict actions, with 97.7% average success across more than 100 tasks. Its test settings run from basic scenes to unseen backgrounds and environments.
figures.credit: Paper figure: Chi-Lam Cheang et al. / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: Three blocks of generated video frames of a robot gripper and objects, each with its instruction and a short evaluator note; after contact, the manipulated object breaks apart or turns into a yellow smear.
figures.caption: Video world models still fail at contact: after the robot touches it, the manipulated object disintegrates or morphs into artifacts. RoboWorld's VLM evaluator catches such rollouts and gives them a dedicated score.
figures.credit: Paper figure: Byeongguk Jeon et al. / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: A grid of five rows of camera frames of a white Franka robot arm on a cluttered lab bench, in columns labelled Start Frame, Subgoal 1, Subgoal 2 and Goal Frame, as the arm picks up a cup and places it.
figures.caption: V-JEPA 2-AC plans in embedding space: on Franka arms in labs absent from its training data, it reaches image goals by comparing predicted representations. Pick and place adds two subgoal images between the start and goal frames.
figures.credit: Paper figure: Mido Assran et al. / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: A flow diagram: internet video and images feed video pretraining of V-JEPA 2, which branches to language alignment, attentive probe training and, with robot data of states and actions, action-conditioned post-training for planning and robot manipulation.
figures.caption: V-JEPA 2 learns from video first and actions second: masked representation prediction on over 1 million hours of internet video and images, then an action-conditioned predictor trained on under 62 hours of robot video.
figures.credit: Paper figure: Mido Assran et al. / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: A grid of rendered simulation tasks: red robot arms reaching, pushing and opening objects on tables, articulated stick figures on checkered floors, and robotic hands manipulating objects.
figures.caption: Latent dynamics models learn a compact state and plan or train inside it. TD-MPC2 plans through such a model with no image decoder; these are initial states from its 104 continuous-control tasks.
figures.credit: Paper figure: Nicklas Hansen et al. / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: A UR5 robot arm with a black gripper above two bins on a table, with three coloured balls in the bins and a colourful picture behind them.
figures.caption: DayDreamer's UR5 learned multi-object visual pick and place from third-person camera images and sparse rewards within a few hours of autonomous operation, training a Dreamer world model on the real robot without a simulator.
figures.credit: Photo: Philipp Wu et al. / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: A black and yellow Unitree A1 quadruped robot lying on its side on a grey floor, legs bent, with a cable trailing behind it.
figures.caption: With a Dreamer-style world model, a Unitree A1 that started on its back learned to roll over, stand up and walk in about one hour of real-world training. A frame from the DayDreamer experiment.
figures.credit: Photo: Philipp Wu et al. / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: Two real tabletop robot images with instructions, wipe the table and remove the bowl from the plate, each turned into a row of generated frames set in a spacecraft interior and a disaster site, with a generalist robot policy acting in the loop.
figures.caption: A neural simulator can stage scenes no lab has. RoboWorld turns real robot images into spacecraft interiors and disaster sites and runs closed-loop policy evaluation inside the generated rollouts.
figures.credit: Paper figure: Byeongguk Jeon et al. / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: Two rows of frames of a simulated four-legged robot, labelled True and Model: two context frames, then open-loop predictions from step 10 to step 50 in which the model row closely tracks the true row.
figures.caption: A world model predicts how an environment evolves under actions. From 5 context frames and the actions alone, DreamerV3 predicts 45 frames of a simulated quadruped; the model row tracks the true row.
figures.credit: Paper figure: Danijar Hafner et al. / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: Two rows of ALOHA robot frames with arrows between them: putting an object on a plate, folding a shirt, putting candies in a bowl and putting candy in a zip bag.
figures.caption: Cosmos Policy fine-tunes a pretrained video model into a robot policy, so a predictive model becomes the controller. Rollouts on four ALOHA tasks, from folding a shirt to putting candy in a zip bag.
figures.credit: Paper figure: Moo Jin Kim et al. / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: A photorealistic rendered view of a garden: a round wooden table with a vase on it, a paved patio, shrubs and a brick wall.
figures.caption: A 3D Gaussian Splatting reconstruction is a learned renderer: it predicts a real scene from a new camera pose by rasterising the fitted Gaussians. A garden scene rendered by the original method.
figures.credit: Paper figure: Bernhard Kerbl et al. / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: Rows of identical simulated white robot arms on grey tables, each with a small green part to assemble, with two insets enlarging a gear and a peg.
figures.caption: A physics simulator integrates explicit geometry, dynamics and contact rules, and steps many copies at once. Assembly environments in Isaac Lab, each an arm with a part to insert, run in parallel on the GPU.
figures.credit: Paper figure: NVIDIA et al. / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: A photorealistic rendered view of a garden: a round wooden table with a vase on it, a paved patio, shrubs and a brick wall.
figures.caption: A 3D Gaussian Splatting reconstruction is a learned renderer: it predicts a real scene from a new camera pose by rasterising the fitted Gaussians. A garden scene rendered by the original method.
figures.credit: Paper figure: Bernhard Kerbl et al. / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: A white robot arm with a gripper above a plate of parts, labelled Robot Setup, beside a grid of close-up photographs of green parts inserted into black fixtures, labelled Successful Assemblies.
figures.caption: Either kind of simulator earns trust only against the same real tasks. The Isaac Lab assembly tasks on a real arm, with its successful assemblies.
figures.credit: Paper figure: NVIDIA et al. / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: A white and black Leica laser tracker on a tripod aims a red laser line at the inside of a large rust-coloured steel ring in a factory hall.
figures.caption: A Leica ATS600 laser tracker measuring a large steel part. Kinematic calibration relies on external instruments like this for its measurement step, recording where the tool really is.
figures.credit: Photo: FanchonH / Wikimedia Commons. Licence: CC BY-SA 4.0.

figures.alt: Close view of a red Baxter robot arm's wrist, with a small camera lens above a two-finger parallel gripper, in an office with computers behind it.
figures.caption: Baxter's wrist carries a camera beside its gripper. Hand-eye calibration solves AX = XB for the fixed transform between that camera and the gripper.
figures.credit: Photo: Gustavo A. Casañ / Wikimedia Commons. Licence: CC BY-SA 4.0.

figures.alt: A cast-iron centrifugal governor: two heavy balls hang from arms on a vertical spindle topped by a coiled spring, linked by levers toward the engine valve gear.
figures.caption: The centrifugal governor of the mill engine at Queen Street Mill, Burnley. As the engine speeds up the balls swing outward and the linkage closes the steam valve, a mechanical feedback loop.
figures.credit: Photo: Clem Rutter / Wikimedia Commons. Licence: CC BY 3.0.

figures.alt: The hydraulic Atlas humanoid robot stands in a lab during testing, with its exposed metal frame, hoses and sensor head visible and its forearms ending without hands.
figures.caption: The hydraulic Atlas during 2013 testing, before its hands were fitted. Kuindersma and colleagues built its controller from optimizations running from footstep placement down to whole-body control.
figures.credit: Photo: DARPA / Wikimedia Commons. Licence: Public domain.

figures.alt: A Rethink Robotics Baxter, a two-armed red and black robot with a screen showing cartoon eyes, stands at a trade-show booth.
figures.caption: Rethink Robotics' Baxter at Innorobo 2015. Its joints drive through series elastic actuators, so a measured spring deflection gives the arm the force channel a stiff geared arm lacks.
figures.credit: Photo: Scailyna / Wikimedia Commons. Licence: CC BY-SA 4.0.

figures.alt: A Care-O-bot service robot with a white and dark grey body extends an orange jointed arm and a multi-fingered hand to grasp a white cylinder on a folding table.
figures.caption: A Care-O-bot service robot grasping a cylinder in 2010. A grasp planner chooses where its fingertips touch so the hold resists pushes and pulls from every direction.
figures.credit: Photo: Jiuguang Wang / Wikimedia Commons. Licence: CC BY-SA 2.0.

figures.alt: A black five-fingered Schunk SVH robot hand silhouetted against a window, fingers spread, with the joints and links of each finger visible.
figures.caption: The Schunk SVH, a servo-electric five-finger hand. Every fingertip or phalanx that touches an object is one contact, and the contact model fixes which forces it can transmit.
figures.credit: Photo: NearEMPTiness / Wikimedia Commons. Licence: CC BY-SA 4.0.

figures.alt: A grey and light blue Universal Robots UR16e arm with six revolute joints, folded over a perforated steel table beside its controller box and a touchscreen teach pendant.
figures.caption: A Universal Robots UR16e, a six-joint serial arm. Forward kinematics composes one transform per joint, so its six joint angles fix the pose of the tool flange.
figures.credit: Photo: Auledas / Wikimedia Commons. Licence: CC BY-SA 4.0.

figures.alt: A stroboscopic NASA photograph shows a PUMA 560 robot arm in several successive positions as it moves small parts between fixtures on a table.
figures.caption: A PUMA 560 at NASA Ames, photographed in a stroboscopic exposure as it cycles through its workspace. The six-revolute PUMA layout is the canonical teaching example for the Denavit-Hartenberg convention.
figures.credit: Photo: NASA / Dominic Hart / Wikimedia Commons. Licence: Public domain.

figures.alt: A white two-armed PR2 robot stands at a round red table in an office, reaching toward small objects, with a whiteboard and computer monitors behind it.
figures.caption: A Willow Garage PR2 in 2010. The TrajOpt benchmark below planned 198 arm problems and 96 full-body problems for this robot in simulated MoveIt scenes.
figures.credit: Photo: Steve Jurvetson / Wikimedia Commons. Licence: CC BY 2.0.

figures.alt: A simulated black Atlas humanoid robot stands at a table in a grey virtual warehouse, holding a red hose toward a green valve wheel on a wall.
figures.caption: A 2013 Defense Department rendering of a simulated Atlas connecting a hose, a DARPA Robotics Challenge task. TrajOpt planned statically stable walking for this 34-DoF humanoid.
figures.credit: Photo: U.S. Department of Defense / Wikimedia Commons. Licence: Public domain.

figures.alt: An Intel RealSense D435 depth camera, a slim grey bar with two infrared lenses, a projector window and a colour camera, mounted on a small tripod.
figures.caption: An Intel RealSense D435, an active stereo camera common on manipulation rigs. Its projector adds texture so matching works on blank surfaces, and its depth error grows with the square of distance.
figures.credit: Photo: Marc Auledas / Wikimedia Commons. Licence: CC BY-SA 4.0.

figures.alt: A black Kinect for Xbox One sensor bar, angled on a white background, with its camera window at one end and a ventilation grille along its top.
figures.caption: The Kinect for Xbox One measured depth by time of flight, the principle its successor Azure Kinect kept. Multi-path light and weak infrared returns invalidate pixels on both.
figures.credit: Photo: Evan-Amos / Wikimedia Commons. Licence: Public domain.

figures.alt: A white two-armed PR2 robot with raised grippers stands at a Maker Faire booth under banners for PR2, TurtleBot and ROS.
figures.caption: A Willow Garage PR2 under the ROS banner at Maker Faire 2011. Willow Garage developed ROS alongside this robot, and ROS 2 is its rebuild for production use.
figures.credit: Photo: Timothy Vollmer / Wikimedia Commons. Licence: CC BY 2.0.

figures.alt: A small black and yellow four-wheeled Clearpath Jackal ground robot with a cylindrical lidar and cameras on its top deck, parked on gravel.
figures.caption: A Clearpath Jackal at the University of Texas robotics center in 2020. Wheeled research bases like it run Nav2, whose planner, controller and recovery servers are ordinary ROS 2 nodes.
figures.credit: Photo: U.S. Army / Luke J. Allen / Wikimedia Commons. Licence: Public domain.

figures.alt: An oblique overhead view of a city intersection drawn entirely in coloured lidar points, with building facades, parked cars and road markings in purple, pink and orange on black.
figures.caption: About 23 million lidar points of a San Francisco intersection, captured in 18 seconds by an Ouster OS1 on a moving car and registered by SLAM. A point cloud is the first rung of the ladder below.
figures.credit: Photo: Daniel L. Lu / Wikimedia Commons. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: A black Kinect for Xbox 360 sensor bar on its pivoting stand, lying on a green cutting mat with its cables coiled beside it.
figures.caption: A first-generation Kinect for Xbox 360. KinectFusion fused this sensor's 640×480 depth frames at 30 Hz into a truncated signed-distance volume on one GPU.
figures.credit: Photo: Antonio Roberts / Wikimedia Commons. Licence: CC BY-SA 2.0.

figures.alt: A Velodyne HDL-64E lidar spinning on a car roof, its cylindrical housing blurred by rotation, above a yellow laser warning label.
figures.caption: A Velodyne HDL-64E on Junior 2, Stanford's autonomous Volkswagen, in 2009. Its 64 spinning beams return over a million points a second, the raw input of a lidar SLAM front end.
figures.credit: Photo: Steve Jurvetson / Wikimedia Commons. Licence: CC BY 2.0.

figures.alt: An Apollo inertial measurement unit on display with its round outer case open, showing the gimballed stable platform with its gyroscopes and accelerometers inside.
figures.caption: An Apollo inertial measurement unit at Draper's 2019 Hack the Moon exhibit. Its gyroscopes and accelerometers integrate motion and drift over time, so an estimator must correct them with outside measurements.
figures.credit: Photo: ArnoldReinhold / Wikimedia Commons. Licence: CC BY-SA 4.0.

figures.alt: The Apollo Guidance Computer, a flat gold-coloured metal case, beside its display and keyboard unit with a numeric keypad and status lights, on a blue background.
figures.caption: The Apollo Guidance Computer and its display and keyboard. Apollo used Potter's square-root form of the Kalman filter, with ground radar as primary navigation and the onboard system as backup.
figures.credit: Photo: NASA / Wikimedia Commons. Licence: Public domain.

figures.alt: The 2013 DARPA Atlas humanoid robot stands facing forward with its exposed metal frame, hydraulic lines, and stereo camera head visible.
figures.caption: The original Atlas humanoid, built for the 2013 DARPA Robotics Challenge: hydraulically actuated, tethered, with its frame and sensor head exposed. The electric Atlas discussed above is its clean-sheet successor.
figures.credit: Photo: DARPA / Wikimedia Commons. Licence: Public domain.

figures.alt: A stroboscopic NASA photograph shows a PUMA 560 robot arm in several successive positions as it moves small parts between fixtures on a table.
figures.caption: A PUMA 560 at NASA Ames, photographed in a stroboscopic exposure as it cycles through its workspace. The six-revolute PUMA layout is the canonical teaching example for the Denavit-Hartenberg convention.
figures.credit: Photo: NASA / Dominic Hart / Wikimedia Commons. Licence: Public domain.

figures.alt: A red and grey ANYmal quadruped robot stands on a metal grate walkway inside an industrial facility, surrounded by pipes and machinery.
figures.caption: ANYmal, the ANYbotics quadruped behind the ETH Zurich locomotion lineage, on an industrial inspection floor. The actuator-network and terrain-curriculum results above all ran on this platform.
figures.credit: Photo: ANYbotics / Wikimedia Commons. Licence: CC BY-SA 4.0.

figures.alt: A white seven-axis Franka Emika Panda robot arm mounted on a demonstration table at CeBIT 2017, guided by hand above trays of small parts.
figures.caption: The Franka Emika Panda, the seven-DoF research arm, demonstrated at CeBIT 2017 with a human guiding it by hand.
figures.credit: Photo: Ims / Wikimedia Commons. Licence: CC BY-SA 4.0.

figures.alt: Diagram of covariate shift: demonstration trajectories form a narrow corridor around the expert path, while the policy rollout starts inside the corridor and drifts outside it.
figures.caption: Robots trained by copying only learn the situations they were shown; one slip lands them somewhere new, where slips grow.
figures.credit: Diagram: Robot Wiki contributors / Robot Wiki (original diagram). Licence: CC BY 4.0.
figures.label: Original schematic

figures.alt: Diagram of temporal ensembling: three overlapping action chunks each contain a prediction for the same action a_t, and oldest-to-newest unnormalized weights are 1.00, 0.61, and 0.37 for illustrative m=0.5; the reference code uses m=0.01.
figures.caption: Blending several overlapping plans smooths the robot’s motion, so one odd prediction jerks the arm less.
figures.credit: Diagram: Robot Wiki contributors / Robot Wiki (original diagram). Licence: CC BY 4.0.
figures.label: Original schematic

figures.alt: A rendered ALOHA 2 workcell: two pairs of black robot arms facing each other across a table inside an aluminium frame with overhead cameras, with letters A, B and C marking measured segments.
figures.caption: ACT was introduced with ALOHA, a low-cost bimanual rig on which a person demonstrates by moving leader arms. A render of the ALOHA 2 workcell, with its frame segments labelled A, B and C.
figures.credit: Paper figure: Tony Z. Zhao et al. / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: Five photographs of ALOHA 2 bimanual robot arms at work, labelled Robot Finger Replace, Shirt Hanging, Gear Insertion, Shoelace Tying and Kitchen Stacking.
figures.caption: Chunked policies now do dexterous bimanual work such as tying shoelaces and hanging shirts. ALOHA Unleashed collected over 26,000 demonstrations for these five tasks on ALOHA 2 and ran each predicted chunk open loop.
figures.credit: Paper figure: Tony Z. Zhao et al. / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: Photographs of two robot platforms, labelled AgileX PiPER Single/Dual Arm Platform and AIRBOT Platform, with arrows marking the head and wrist camera views.
figures.caption: The two arm platforms of an action-space study with more than 13,000 real rollouts and 500+ models. Predicting delta actions consistently helped; joint space favoured control stability and task space favoured generalisation.
figures.credit: Paper figure: Yuchun Feng et al. / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: Two photographs, each beside a line drawing: a robot arm pushes a blue box up against a block, with arrows marking a high stiffness K1 and a low stiffness K2, and two arms hold and wipe a white vase, with arrows marking compliance directions.
figures.caption: An impedance action sets the robot's stiffness in each direction as well as its goal. Adaptive Compliance Policy flips an item, soft (K2) along the push and stiff (K1) elsewhere, and wipes a vase with both arms compliant.
figures.credit: Paper figure: Yifan Hou et al. / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: A labelled photograph of the DROID data collection rig: a Franka Panda arm on a height-adjustable desk with two side-mounted Zed 2 cameras, a wrist camera and an Oculus Quest 2 headset with controllers.
figures.caption: Behavior cloning starts from demonstrations recorded on rigs like this one, where a person teleoperates the arm through a VR headset. DROID used this Franka Panda setup at every institution.
figures.credit: Paper figure: Alexander Khazatsky et al. / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: Five Carnegie Mellon Navlab autonomous research vehicles parked in a row, from the first Navlab van in the back to the Navlab 5 minivan in front.
figures.caption: Behavior cloning began on the road: ALVINN learned to steer the Navlab van by watching a human driver. Navlab 1 (back) through Navlab 5 (front), built at Carnegie Mellon University from 1984 to 1995.
figures.credit: Photo: Firefly4342 / Wikimedia Commons. Licence: CC BY-SA 4.0.

figures.alt: Nine photographs of robot setups: WidowX BridgeV2, UR5 Tabletop and RT-1 Robot grouped under 0-Shot Evaluation, and Berkeley Insert, Stanford Coffee, CMU Baking, Berkeley Pick-up, Berkeley Coke and Berkeley Bimanual grouped under Finetuning Evaluation.
figures.caption: Octo, an open-weights policy, was evaluated out of the box on three robot setups and fine-tuned on six more, some with new observations, action spaces or embodiments.
figures.credit: Paper figure: Octo Model Team / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: A diagram of RoboArena: a pool of generalist policies feeds a ring of photographed robot workstations, each running pairwise comparisons on its own task, which aggregate into a ranked score table.
figures.caption: RoboArena ranks policies from double-blind pairwise trials that many evaluators run on their own scenes and tasks. More than 600 real-robot episodes on the DROID platform ranked seven generalist policies.
figures.credit: Paper figure: Pranav Atreya et al. / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: Two rows of frames: an Apptronik Apollo humanoid robot packs a lunch bag, and a bi-arm industrial Franka setup fits a rubber band around a pulley system.
figures.caption: One Gemini Robotics model was fine-tuned to drive very different bodies, from the Apollo humanoid packing a lunch bag (top) to a bi-arm Franka fitting a rubber band around pulleys (bottom).
figures.credit: Paper figure: Gemini Robotics Team / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: An infographic framed by robot dataset thumbnails reading 1M episodes from 311 scenes, 34 research labs across 21 institutions, 22 embodiments, 527 skills and 60 datasets.
figures.caption: Open X-Embodiment pooled robot data into one training set: 1M episodes from 60 datasets, 22 embodiments and 527 skills, contributed by 34 labs at 21 institutions.
figures.credit: Paper figure: Open X-Embodiment Collaboration / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: A three-stage diagram with photographs: egocentric human videos of hands doing chores, paired human and robot play data, and a humanoid robot hand performing dexterous tasks after post-training.
figures.caption: EgoScale pretrains on human video, mid-trains on aligned human and robot play, then post-trains on robot tasks. The pretraining stage uses 20,854 hours of egocentric video with wrist motion and retargeted hand actions.
figures.credit: Paper figure: Ruijie Zheng et al. / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: A pipeline of photographs: a human hand demonstrates a task, the hand is inpainted out of the video, a rendered robot gripper is overlaid in its place, and a real robot then performs the task.
figures.caption: Phantom trains a robot policy without robot data by erasing the human hand from demonstration videos and rendering a robot arm in its pose. The policy then deploys zero-shot on a real robot, with success up to 92%.
figures.credit: Paper figure: Marion Lepert et al. / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: Six labelled frames of two robot arms hanging a red shirt: initial state, orient shirt, pick hanger, insert right collar, insert left collar and hang on rack.
figures.caption: A diffusion policy hangs a shirt on its own, a long-horizon task with a deformable object and several bimanual stages. Six frames of an autonomous ALOHA Unleashed rollout, from the initial state to the shirt on the rack.
figures.credit: Paper figure: Tony Z. Zhao et al. / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: Two photographs: everyday objects on a wooden table with the letters DP3 spelled out, and a Franka arm with an Allegro hand and a RealSense L515 camera above a table.
figures.caption: 3D Diffusion Policy swaps images for sparse point clouds from a single depth camera. Left, the everyday objects in its real tasks; right, a Franka arm with an Allegro hand under a RealSense L515.
figures.credit: Paper figure: Yanjie Ze et al. / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: Photographs of the robot arms RoboCat controls, each labelled with its action dimensions: Sawyer and Panda arms with parallel grippers seen in training, and a KUKA arm with a three-finger hand held out for fine-tuning.
figures.caption: An adaptation budget is part of a foundation claim: RoboCat learned Sawyer and Panda arms in training and met the KUKA arm with a three-finger hand only at fine-tuning, from 100 to 1,000 examples.
figures.credit: Paper figure: Konstantinos Bousmalis et al. / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: Rows of frames from a Fourier GR-1 humanoid robot at a wooden table handing objects between its hands, placing a peach in a bin and moving items onto plates and into baskets.
figures.caption: GR00T N1 runs a vision-language model at 10 Hz over a 120 Hz action module on the GR-1 humanoid. Frames from real rollouts: pretraining evaluations (top) and post-trained pick-and-place and articulated-object tasks (bottom).
figures.credit: Paper figure: NVIDIA et al. / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: Two rows of ALOHA robot frames with arrows between them: putting an object on a plate, folding a shirt, putting candies in a bowl and putting candy in a zip bag.
figures.caption: Cosmos Policy fine-tunes a pretrained video model into a robot policy, so a predictive model becomes the controller. Rollouts on four ALOHA tasks, from folding a shirt to putting candy in a zip bag.
figures.credit: Paper figure: Moo Jin Kim et al. / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: Four rows of overhead frames of two robot grippers opening an eyeglasses case, pouring pulses, unfastening a file folder and wrapping a headphone wire on a cluttered table.
figures.caption: A vision-language-action model performs dexterous bimanual work in clutter. Gemini Robotics on ALOHA, top to bottom: open the eyeglasses case, pour pulses, unfasten a file folder and wrap a headphone wire.
figures.credit: Paper figure: Gemini Robotics Team / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: Two rows of frames of a robot arm pouring from a paper cup into a bowl and wiping a table with a sponge, each labelled with language motions such as rotate arm left and move arm forward and left.
figures.caption: RT-H first predicts a language motion such as "rotate arm left", then the action, so a person can correct the motion in words. Frames from two unseen tasks, with and without such corrections.
figures.credit: Paper figure: Suneel Belkhale et al. / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: Two pairs of photographs of real robot tabletop scenes, each with a coloured path drawn from the gripper towards its target: screwing a light bulb into a lamp, and pushing coloured buttons in order.
figures.caption: HAMSTER's high level draws a coarse 2D path for the gripper, and a low-level policy turns the path into motion. Paths predicted on real scenes run from blue to red; blue and red circles mark grasp and release.
figures.credit: Paper figure: Yi Li et al. / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: A strip of frames from a robot camera showing a mobile robot clearing dishes, cups and trash from a table into a bin.
figures.caption: Table bussing is the task behind KI's training-cost result: a many-embodiment π0 generalist needed 7.5 times the training steps of π0.5 with KI to reach similar performance. Frames of the task from the FAST paper.
figures.credit: Paper figure: Karl Pertsch et al. / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: An overhead view of two robot arms folding a flat cardboard sheet into a box on a table.
figures.caption: π0.6, whose card lists a Gemma3 4B backbone with an insulated expert of about 860M parameters, building a box. Physical Intelligence used this task to test training-time real-time chunking.
figures.credit: Photo: Kevin Black et al. / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: A close view of robot grippers at an espresso station, one holding a portafilter filled with ground coffee next to a tamping stand.
figures.caption: A π0.6 policy making espresso on Physical Intelligence's bimanual rig. The pi line runs one vision-language backbone with a flow-matching action expert across tasks like this one.
figures.credit: Photo: Kevin Black et al. / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: A strip of frames showing two robot arms taking a shirt from a basket, spreading it on a table and folding it.
figures.caption: Laundry folding is the kind of high-frequency task FAST was built for: with naive per-step tokens, policies made no progress on T-shirt folding at 50 Hz. Frames of the task from the FAST paper.
figures.credit: Paper figure: Karl Pertsch et al. / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: A robot gripper holds a freshly struck match above a pie with a candle in it, while a second gripper holds the open matchbox.
figures.caption: Real-time chunking lets a robot strike a match and light a candle despite inference delays above 300 ms, more than 30% of the model's prediction horizon. A frame from the RTC paper's candle task.
figures.credit: Photo: Kevin Black et al. / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: An NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin developer kit, a compact black and silver module with a heat sink, beside its retail box on a white background.
figures.caption: On-robot compute such as the NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin developer kit sets the hardware wall: a policy that fits a desktop GPU's budget can miss the control tick here.
figures.credit: Photo: Auledas / Wikimedia Commons. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: Four photographs of robot arms whipping a block out of a Jenga tower, flipping an object in a pan, assembling a timing belt and fitting a car dashboard.
figures.caption: Reinforcement learning on the real robot reaches precise, dynamic skills that demonstrations alone struggle with. Four of the HIL-SERL tasks: Jenga whipping, object flipping in a pan, timing-belt assembly and dashboard assembly.
figures.credit: Paper figure: Jianlan Luo et al. / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: Photographs of a Franka arm picking up a blue cube and plugging in a yellow peg, and of bimanual arms inserting a GPU card into a motherboard slot in four stages.
figures.caption: PLD trains a residual RL policy on top of a frozen VLA and distills the improved behavior back into it. On bimanual YAM arms the result ran GPU insertion and unplugging for a continuous hour without human resets.
figures.credit: Paper figure: Wenli Xiao et al. / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: Eight labelled photographs of a Franka arm picking a banana, a spoon and bread, opening a drawer and a toaster, putting bread in a toaster, inserting a chair wheel and hanging a Chinese knot.
figures.caption: ConRFT fine-tunes a VLA with real-world reinforcement learning across eight contact-rich tasks, from picking a banana to inserting a chair wheel and hanging a Chinese knot.
figures.credit: Paper figure: Yuhui Chen et al. / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: A black Unimate PUMA 500 industrial robot arm from 1983 on a museum plinth, beside its Unimation control cabinet and a computer terminal.
figures.caption: Every learned policy still runs through coordinate frames like those of this Unimate PUMA 500 (1983), an industrial arm whose kinematics became the textbook example. Exhibit at the Deutsches Museum, Munich.
figures.credit: Photo: Theoprakt / Wikimedia Commons. Licence: CC BY-SA 3.0.

figures.alt: A grid of robot camera frames grouped by scene type, showing the same Franka arm working in kitchens, bedrooms, bathrooms, offices, laundry rooms and other real buildings.
figures.caption: Every stage of the curriculum meets real robot data like DROID's: 76k trajectories from 13 institutions, recorded with one Franka setup in kitchens, bedrooms, offices and other real buildings. Example frames grouped into the dataset's 9 scene types.
figures.credit: Paper figure: Alexander Khazatsky et al. / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: A grid of rendered simulated kitchens in different layouts and styles, each with a robot standing among cabinets, counters and appliances.
figures.caption: Simulation lets a team test policies across many environments before touching hardware. Rendered RoboCasa kitchens, each holding a simulated robot among varied layouts and styles.
figures.credit: Paper figure: Soroush Nasiriany et al. / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: Two rows of frames of a simulated four-legged robot, labelled True and Model: two context frames, then open-loop predictions from step 10 to step 50 in which the model row closely tracks the true row.
figures.caption: A world model predicts how an environment evolves under actions. From 5 context frames and the actions alone, DreamerV3 predicts 45 frames of a simulated quadruped; the model row tracks the true row.
figures.credit: Paper figure: Danijar Hafner et al. / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: A photorealistic rendered view of a garden: a round wooden table with a vase on it, a paved patio, shrubs and a brick wall.
figures.caption: A 3D Gaussian Splatting reconstruction is a learned renderer: it predicts a real scene from a new camera pose by rasterising the fitted Gaussians. A garden scene rendered by the original method.
figures.credit: Paper figure: Bernhard Kerbl et al. / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: A grid of rendered simulation tasks: red robot arms reaching, pushing and opening objects on tables, articulated stick figures on checkered floors, and robotic hands manipulating objects.
figures.caption: Latent dynamics models learn a compact state and plan or train inside it. TD-MPC2 plans through such a model with no image decoder; these are initial states from its 104 continuous-control tasks.
figures.credit: Paper figure: Nicklas Hansen et al. / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: A UR5 robot arm with a black gripper above two bins on a table, with three coloured balls in the bins and a colourful picture behind them.
figures.caption: DayDreamer's UR5 learned multi-object visual pick and place from third-person camera images and sparse rewards within a few hours of autonomous operation, training a Dreamer world model on the real robot without a simulator.
figures.credit: Photo: Philipp Wu et al. / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: A black and yellow Unitree A1 quadruped robot lying on its side on a grey floor, legs bent, with a cable trailing behind it.
figures.caption: With a Dreamer-style world model, a Unitree A1 that started on its back learned to roll over, stand up and walk in about one hour of real-world training. A frame from the DayDreamer experiment.
figures.credit: Photo: Philipp Wu et al. / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: Two real tabletop robot images with instructions, wipe the table and remove the bowl from the plate, each turned into a row of generated frames set in a spacecraft interior and a disaster site, with a generalist robot policy acting in the loop.
figures.caption: A neural simulator can stage scenes no lab has. RoboWorld turns real robot images into spacecraft interiors and disaster sites and runs closed-loop policy evaluation inside the generated rollouts.
figures.credit: Paper figure: Byeongguk Jeon et al. / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: Three pairs of frame strips for the instructions grasp the blue block and rotate it right, put the broccoli onto the plate, and open the drawer; green-framed ground-truth frames sit above blue-framed predicted frames.
figures.caption: A video world model predicts future frames of a robot task from the current view and a language instruction. GR-1's predicted frames (blue) beneath the ground truth (green) for three instructions.
figures.credit: Paper figure: Hongtao Wu et al. / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: Four groups of tabletop photographs of a robot arm among household objects, labelled Basic Settings, Unseen Backgrounds, Unseen Environments and Unseen Manipulation.
figures.caption: GR-2 pre-trains on web-scale video, then fine-tunes on robot data to generate video and predict actions, with 97.7% average success across more than 100 tasks. Its test settings run from basic scenes to unseen backgrounds and environments.
figures.credit: Paper figure: Chi-Lam Cheang et al. / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: Three blocks of generated video frames of a robot gripper and objects, each with its instruction and a short evaluator note; after contact, the manipulated object breaks apart or turns into a yellow smear.
figures.caption: Video world models still fail at contact: after the robot touches it, the manipulated object disintegrates or morphs into artifacts. RoboWorld's VLM evaluator catches such rollouts and gives them a dedicated score.
figures.credit: Paper figure: Byeongguk Jeon et al. / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: A grid of five rows of camera frames of a white Franka robot arm on a cluttered lab bench, in columns labelled Start Frame, Subgoal 1, Subgoal 2 and Goal Frame, as the arm picks up a cup and places it.
figures.caption: V-JEPA 2-AC plans in embedding space: on Franka arms in labs absent from its training data, it reaches image goals by comparing predicted representations. Pick and place adds two subgoal images between the start and goal frames.
figures.credit: Paper figure: Mido Assran et al. / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: A flow diagram: internet video and images feed video pretraining of V-JEPA 2, which branches to language alignment, attentive probe training and, with robot data of states and actions, action-conditioned post-training for planning and robot manipulation.
figures.caption: V-JEPA 2 learns from video first and actions second: masked representation prediction on over 1 million hours of internet video and images, then an action-conditioned predictor trained on under 62 hours of robot video.
figures.credit: Paper figure: Mido Assran et al. / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: Two panels: real robot evaluation, labelled expensive, slow and difficult to reproduce, with photographs of a robot arm at a table; and simulated evaluation, labelled cheap, scalable and fully reproducible, with matching simulated views.
figures.caption: A cheaper evaluator is useful only if it agrees with reality. SIMPLER builds simulated scenes matched to real ones and checks whether simulated policy performance correlates with real performance; a learned simulator should meet the same test.
figures.credit: Paper figure: Xuanlin Li et al. / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: A grid of video frames of a robot arm pushing objects at steps 0, 8, 14, 21 and 29, with rows for ground truth and five rollout methods; red boxes mark misaligned and blurred frames, and the last row is marked aligned.
figures.caption: Autoregressive rollouts can drift in ways one frame hides. On BAIR robot pushing, the RoboWorld authors mark other forcing schemes misaligned or blurred within 29 steps, while their step forcing stays aligned with the ground truth.
figures.credit: Paper figure: Byeongguk Jeon et al. / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: A rendered kitchen table crowded with hundreds of 3D objects: fruit, vegetables, meat, bottles, cans, cups, cookware and packaged food.
figures.caption: Generative simulation authors content and leaves dynamics to the physics engine. RoboCasa's library holds 2,509 objects in 153 categories, drawn from Objaverse and the text-to-3D service Luma.ai; a small subset is shown here.
figures.credit: Paper figure: Soroush Nasiriany et al. / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: Rows of identical simulated white robot arms on grey tables, each with a small green part to assemble, with two insets enlarging a gear and a peg.
figures.caption: A physics simulator integrates explicit geometry, dynamics and contact rules, and steps many copies at once. Assembly environments in Isaac Lab, each an arm with a part to insert, run in parallel on the GPU.
figures.credit: Paper figure: NVIDIA et al. / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: A white robot arm with a gripper above a plate of parts, labelled Robot Setup, beside a grid of close-up photographs of green parts inserted into black fixtures, labelled Successful Assemblies.
figures.caption: Either kind of simulator earns trust only against the same real tasks. The Isaac Lab assembly tasks on a real arm, with its successful assemblies.
figures.credit: Paper figure: NVIDIA et al. / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: A grey and light blue Universal Robots UR16e arm with six revolute joints, folded over a perforated steel table beside its controller box and a touchscreen teach pendant.
figures.caption: A Universal Robots UR16e, a six-joint serial arm. Forward kinematics composes one transform per joint, so its six joint angles fix the pose of the tool flange.
figures.credit: Photo: Auledas / Wikimedia Commons. Licence: CC BY-SA 4.0.

figures.alt: A white two-armed PR2 robot stands at a round red table in an office, reaching toward small objects, with a whiteboard and computer monitors behind it.
figures.caption: A Willow Garage PR2 in 2010. The TrajOpt benchmark below planned 198 arm problems and 96 full-body problems for this robot in simulated MoveIt scenes.
figures.credit: Photo: Steve Jurvetson / Wikimedia Commons. Licence: CC BY 2.0.

figures.alt: A simulated black Atlas humanoid robot stands at a table in a grey virtual warehouse, holding a red hose toward a green valve wheel on a wall.
figures.caption: A 2013 Defense Department rendering of a simulated Atlas connecting a hose, a DARPA Robotics Challenge task. TrajOpt planned statically stable walking for this 34-DoF humanoid.
figures.credit: Photo: U.S. Department of Defense / Wikimedia Commons. Licence: Public domain.

figures.alt: A cast-iron centrifugal governor: two heavy balls hang from arms on a vertical spindle topped by a coiled spring, linked by levers toward the engine valve gear.
figures.caption: The centrifugal governor of the mill engine at Queen Street Mill, Burnley. As the engine speeds up the balls swing outward and the linkage closes the steam valve, a mechanical feedback loop.
figures.credit: Photo: Clem Rutter / Wikimedia Commons. Licence: CC BY 3.0.

figures.alt: The hydraulic Atlas humanoid robot stands in a lab during testing, with its exposed metal frame, hoses and sensor head visible and its forearms ending without hands.
figures.caption: The hydraulic Atlas during 2013 testing, before its hands were fitted. Kuindersma and colleagues built its controller from optimizations running from footstep placement down to whole-body control.
figures.credit: Photo: DARPA / Wikimedia Commons. Licence: Public domain.

figures.alt: A Rethink Robotics Baxter, a two-armed red and black robot with a screen showing cartoon eyes, stands at a trade-show booth.
figures.caption: Rethink Robotics' Baxter at Innorobo 2015. Its joints drive through series elastic actuators, so a measured spring deflection gives the arm the force channel a stiff geared arm lacks.
figures.credit: Photo: Scailyna / Wikimedia Commons. Licence: CC BY-SA 4.0.

figures.alt: An Apollo inertial measurement unit on display with its round outer case open, showing the gimballed stable platform with its gyroscopes and accelerometers inside.
figures.caption: An Apollo inertial measurement unit at Draper's 2019 Hack the Moon exhibit. Its gyroscopes and accelerometers integrate motion and drift over time, so an estimator must correct them with outside measurements.
figures.credit: Photo: ArnoldReinhold / Wikimedia Commons. Licence: CC BY-SA 4.0.

figures.alt: The Apollo Guidance Computer, a flat gold-coloured metal case, beside its display and keyboard unit with a numeric keypad and status lights, on a blue background.
figures.caption: The Apollo Guidance Computer and its display and keyboard. Apollo used Potter's square-root form of the Kalman filter, with ground radar as primary navigation and the onboard system as backup.
figures.credit: Photo: NASA / Wikimedia Commons. Licence: Public domain.

figures.alt: A Care-O-bot service robot with a white and dark grey body extends an orange jointed arm and a multi-fingered hand to grasp a white cylinder on a folding table.
figures.caption: A Care-O-bot service robot grasping a cylinder in 2010. A grasp planner chooses where its fingertips touch so the hold resists pushes and pulls from every direction.
figures.credit: Photo: Jiuguang Wang / Wikimedia Commons. Licence: CC BY-SA 2.0.

figures.alt: A black five-fingered Schunk SVH robot hand silhouetted against a window, fingers spread, with the joints and links of each finger visible.
figures.caption: The Schunk SVH, a servo-electric five-finger hand. Every fingertip or phalanx that touches an object is one contact, and the contact model fixes which forces it can transmit.
figures.credit: Photo: NearEMPTiness / Wikimedia Commons. Licence: CC BY-SA 4.0.

figures.alt: An Intel RealSense D435 depth camera, a slim grey bar with two infrared lenses, a projector window and a colour camera, mounted on a small tripod.
figures.caption: An Intel RealSense D435, an active stereo camera common on manipulation rigs. Its projector adds texture so matching works on blank surfaces, and its depth error grows with the square of distance.
figures.credit: Photo: Marc Auledas / Wikimedia Commons. Licence: CC BY-SA 4.0.

figures.alt: A black Kinect for Xbox One sensor bar, angled on a white background, with its camera window at one end and a ventilation grille along its top.
figures.caption: The Kinect for Xbox One measured depth by time of flight, the principle its successor Azure Kinect kept. Multi-path light and weak infrared returns invalidate pixels on both.
figures.credit: Photo: Evan-Amos / Wikimedia Commons. Licence: Public domain.

figures.alt: A white and black Leica laser tracker on a tripod aims a red laser line at the inside of a large rust-coloured steel ring in a factory hall.
figures.caption: A Leica ATS600 laser tracker measuring a large steel part. Kinematic calibration relies on external instruments like this for its measurement step, recording where the tool really is.
figures.credit: Photo: FanchonH / Wikimedia Commons. Licence: CC BY-SA 4.0.

figures.alt: Close view of a red Baxter robot arm's wrist, with a small camera lens above a two-finger parallel gripper, in an office with computers behind it.
figures.caption: Baxter's wrist carries a camera beside its gripper. Hand-eye calibration solves AX = XB for the fixed transform between that camera and the gripper.
figures.credit: Photo: Gustavo A. Casañ / Wikimedia Commons. Licence: CC BY-SA 4.0.

figures.alt: A white two-armed PR2 robot with raised grippers stands at a Maker Faire booth under banners for PR2, TurtleBot and ROS.
figures.caption: A Willow Garage PR2 under the ROS banner at Maker Faire 2011. Willow Garage developed ROS alongside this robot, and ROS 2 is its rebuild for production use.
figures.credit: Photo: Timothy Vollmer / Wikimedia Commons. Licence: CC BY 2.0.

figures.alt: A small black and yellow four-wheeled Clearpath Jackal ground robot with a cylindrical lidar and cameras on its top deck, parked on gravel.
figures.caption: A Clearpath Jackal at the University of Texas robotics center in 2020. Wheeled research bases like it run Nav2, whose planner, controller and recovery servers are ordinary ROS 2 nodes.
figures.credit: Photo: U.S. Army / Luke J. Allen / Wikimedia Commons. Licence: Public domain.

figures.alt: An oblique overhead view of a city intersection drawn entirely in coloured lidar points, with building facades, parked cars and road markings in purple, pink and orange on black.
figures.caption: About 23 million lidar points of a San Francisco intersection, captured in 18 seconds by an Ouster OS1 on a moving car and registered by SLAM. A point cloud is the first rung of the ladder below.
figures.credit: Photo: Daniel L. Lu / Wikimedia Commons. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: A black Kinect for Xbox 360 sensor bar on its pivoting stand, lying on a green cutting mat with its cables coiled beside it.
figures.caption: A first-generation Kinect for Xbox 360. KinectFusion fused this sensor's 640×480 depth frames at 30 Hz into a truncated signed-distance volume on one GPU.
figures.credit: Photo: Antonio Roberts / Wikimedia Commons. Licence: CC BY-SA 2.0.

figures.alt: A Velodyne HDL-64E lidar spinning on a car roof, its cylindrical housing blurred by rotation, above a yellow laser warning label.
figures.caption: A Velodyne HDL-64E on Junior 2, Stanford's autonomous Volkswagen, in 2009. Its 64 spinning beams return over a million points a second, the raw input of a lidar SLAM front end.
figures.credit: Photo: Steve Jurvetson / Wikimedia Commons. Licence: CC BY 2.0.

figures.alt: The electric Atlas humanoid by Boston Dynamics, grey and white with a round head and slim jointed limbs, stands on display in a showroom.
figures.caption: The electric Atlas on display at Hyundai Motorstudio Goyang in July 2026. ZEST trains motion-imitation policies on motion capture, video and animation and deploys them on this robot zero-shot.
figures.credit: Photo: Damian B Oh / Wikimedia Commons. Licence: CC BY-SA 4.0.

figures.alt: Performers in black motion capture suits dotted with reflective markers stand in a studio capture volume ringed by cameras, seen mostly from behind.
figures.caption: Optical motion capture records body movement from reflective suit markers seen by a ring of cameras. AMASS pooled 15 such datasets, over 40 hours and 11,000 motions, into one body model that humanoid tracking policies learn to imitate.
figures.credit: Photo: Applearts123 / Wikimedia Commons. Licence: CC BY-SA 4.0.

figures.alt: Unitree robots on a dark exhibition stand: a silver humanoid hangs from a lifting hoist in front, a G1 humanoid with a glowing blue face ring stands behind it, and a quadruped sits on the right.
figures.caption: Unitree robots at Japan Mobility Show 2025, with a G1 behind the hoisted humanoid. GR00T N1.7 drives the G1 through GEAR-SONIC, which decodes its latent action tokens into leg, arm and hand commands at 50 Hz.
figures.credit: Photo: RuinDig/Yuki Uchida / Wikimedia Commons. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: A yellow and black Boston Dynamics Spot quadruped walks along a gravel path through a forest.
figures.caption: Spot, the Boston Dynamics quadruped, outdoors in 2023. Boston Dynamics ships its learned locomotion policy to Spot by software update and reports fewer falls on slick and irregular ground.
figures.credit: Photo: Jonte / Wikimedia Commons. Licence: CC BY-SA 4.0.

figures.alt: A card of twelve sequential silhouette photographs of a horse and rider at a gallop, taken by Eadweard Muybridge in 1878, with printed text beneath the frames.
figures.caption: Eadweard Muybridge's 1878 sequence of a galloping horse caught all four hooves off the ground. A gait is such a footfall timing pattern; Walk These Ways commands it to a robot as phase offsets between foot pairs.
figures.credit: Photo: Eadweard Muybridge / Wikimedia Commons. Licence: Public domain.

figures.alt: Cassie, a bipedal robot with backward-bending legs and no upper body, walks along a forest path while a researcher follows with a handheld controller.
figures.caption: Cassie, the bipedal robot built at Oregon State University, walking in a research forest in 2017. Learned controllers later ran Cassie through a 400-meter dash and composed periodic rewards into standing, walking, hopping, running and skipping.
figures.credit: Photo: Oregon State University / Wikimedia Commons. Licence: CC BY-SA 2.0.

figures.alt: An ANYmal X quadruped robot climbs down a steel staircase on an offshore platform, surrounded by railings and industrial piping.
figures.caption: ANYmal X descending stairs on an offshore rig during an inspection round in 2022. The ANYmal line is where simulation-trained locomotion policies first transferred to hardware, in 2019.
figures.credit: Photo: Cvoellmy / Wikimedia Commons. Licence: CC BY-SA 4.0.

figures.alt: The Shadow Dexterous Hand, a humanlike robot hand with visible joints and tendons, holds a light bulb between its fingertips.
figures.caption: The Shadow Dexterous Hand holding a light bulb in 2007. Each fingertip is a contact whose geometry and friction a simulator must get right; a modified Shadow hand ran the Rubik's cube policy trained with automatic domain randomization.
figures.credit: Photo: Richard Greenhill and Hugo Elias, Shadow Robot Company / Wikimedia Commons. Licence: CC BY-SA 3.0.

figures.alt: A rendered Shadow Hand holding a cube in the foreground, with rows of identical hand and object environments receding behind it across a grey checkered floor.
figures.caption: Isaac Gym's Shadow Hand task, rendered with many copies of the same hand and cube stepped together on one GPU. Its authors report 2 to 3 orders of magnitude improvement over a CPU simulator feeding a GPU network.
figures.credit: Paper figure: Viktor Makoviychuk et al. / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: Rendered robots from MuJoCo Playground arranged together: a Berkeley Humanoid, Unitree Go1 and G1, a LEAP hand and a Franka arm.
figures.caption: MuJoCo Playground environments that transferred to real hardware: the Berkeley Humanoid, Unitree Go1 and G1, the LEAP hand and a Franka arm. The framework runs MuJoCo on the GPU through MJX, with sim-to-real transfer as an express goal.
figures.credit: Paper figure: Kevin Zakka et al. / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: The MIT Mini Cheetah, a small silver quadruped on a safety tether, spins in place on foam floor mats, its legs blurred by motion.
figures.caption: The MIT Mini Cheetah spinning at 5.7 rad/s under a policy trained in simulation, 90% of the 6.28 rad/s yaw rate a model-based controller reached on the robot. The same network sprints at 3.9 m/s.
figures.credit: Photo: Gabriel B. Margolis et al. / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: A rendered grid of terrain tiles with stairs, slopes and rough ground, covered with many ANYmal quadrupeds training at once against a black background.
figures.caption: ANYmal robots training in parallel on Isaac Gym stairs and slopes, laid out as tiles of rising difficulty. The curriculum promotes robots that cross a tile and demotes those that cover under half the commanded distance.
figures.credit: Paper figure: Viktor Makoviychuk et al. / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: Overlaid frames show a Unitree A1 quadruped on a lab floor being pushed with a long tube and keeping or regaining its footing.
figures.caption: DayDreamer's Unitree A1 learned to roll over, stand and walk in one hour on the real robot with no simulator. Within ten more minutes of pushes it learned to withstand them or roll back onto its feet.
figures.credit: Photo: Philipp Wu et al. / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: Rendered Allegro robot hands, each turning a cube, repeated across a large grid of parallel simulation environments on a grey checkered floor.
figures.caption: Isaac Gym's Allegro hand task, one hand and cube per environment, all stepped together on a GPU. When steps cost this little, training stability becomes the scarce resource, which is why GPU-simulation work defaulted to PPO.
figures.credit: Paper figure: Viktor Makoviychuk et al. / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: A rendered TriFinger robot: three robotic fingers mounted above a round, walled arena push a cube toward a target pose.
figures.caption: TriFinger, three robot fingers over a round arena, rendered in Isaac Gym. The real benchmark pairs reproducible hardware with simulation for debugging, so offline-RL policies trained on its fixed datasets meet the same robot every time.
figures.credit: Paper figure: Viktor Makoviychuk et al. / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: Three robot scenes in four columns labelled Real, Raw Sim, Sim plus Green Screen, and Sim plus Green Screen plus Texture Matching; the simulated views grow closer to the real camera images from left to right.
figures.caption: SIMPLER matches its simulated scenes to real camera views, from raw simulation to a green-screened real background with matched textures. The authors checked simulated rankings against paired real evaluations before trusting them.
figures.credit: Paper figure: Xuanlin Li et al. / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: A red and black ANYmal quadruped climbs a short flight of carpeted steps inside an office building, with wooden blocks on the floor nearby.
figures.caption: A real ANYmal climbing indoor steps with a rough-terrain policy trained in Isaac Gym. The Isaac Gym paper shows the same policy on simulated terrain beside this hardware test.
figures.credit: Photo: Viktor Makoviychuk et al. / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

figures.alt: A real Franka Emika Panda arm with a Robotiq gripper pushes a foam yoga block across a table toward a marked goal region.
figures.caption: A Franka Panda pushes a yoga block to a goal with a MuJoCo Playground policy trained under domain randomization and transferred zero-shot. Early policies moved fast enough to trip the arm's force limit, so the authors added torque penalties.
figures.credit: Photo: Kevin Zakka et al. / arXiv. Licence: CC BY 4.0.
